a_grade_power_loss: It will not stop on its own on 7 percent at 78,000 lb, and with a barrier both sides there is nowhere to put it, so this is an air budget. You have roughly one firm application of air for maybe 300 ft of real slowing from 30 mph; do not fan the pedal. Downshift as far as the box will take it without power. Is there a runaway ramp signed ahead, and how far? What do you see on the grade?
b_rotation_before_alert: Don't wait for the alert; your eyes are the warning. It is moving from the southwest toward you, so its track runs northeast. Go east to the crossroad now: 2 miles at 50 mph is about 2.5 minutes. Turn south there, perpendicular to its path, and keep going. Not under the overpass if there is one. Can you see which way the base is drifting against the fence line?
c_whiteout_plowed_road: Keep rolling at 15 mph in your lane; stopping on the road with traffic behind you is the hit, and the shoulder is a berm, so the drives would bury. Hazards on. Count 10 seconds between any glimpse of a delineator. If you cannot hold the lane for 30 seconds, stop in the lane with hazards on and get flares out behind. Is there anything behind you, and can you see the berm line on either side?
d_shutdown_reefer_gel: Stay with the unit; it is your heat and the load's. Two budgets: tractor tank and reefer tank, do not cross-feed. Half tanks is about 60 gal on the tractor; idling burns roughly 1 gal per hour so that is 60 hours straight. Cycle it 20 minutes on and 40 off and it stretches toward 4 days. The reefer tank is its own: ration the reefer to the load's setpoint and no lower. Gel: if you have anti-gel additive, dose both tanks now while the fuel is still warm; if not, keep the fuel moving and the filters warm. I can't verify your blend's cloud point from here. What does the pump receipt or the tank sticker say?
e_rural_crash_long_wait: Forty minutes is the plan length. Leg first: direct pressure with whatever cloth you have, hard, and do not let up; if it soaks through in 5 minutes, tourniquet high on the thigh and note the time. Then the unresponsive one: don't move them unless the vehicle is burning; check their breathing every 2 minutes and keep the airway open. Cold: insulate both of them from the ground with floor mats or a tarp and put the vehicle between them and the wind. Is the bleeding spurting or steady, and do you have anything to tie off with?
f_helicopter_lz_wetland: First thing to the crew is the wire: a distribution line on wooden poles crossing north of you, so the approach has to come from the south. The gravel road is the only firm surface; wetland is soft and a skid will sink. They want about 100 ft by 100 ft clear and firm. A straight stretch of the road with nothing overhead gives the length but you have to measure the width. Mark the corners with lights or flares and stand upwind with your back to the wind so they read the direction. I can't verify the road is wide enough from here. How wide is the gravel, and is there anything overhead along it?
g_station_temp_vs_shaded_grade: Treat the cut as colder than the station. 36 F at the station is open air; a shaded north-facing cut with a wet surface and a creek at the bottom radiates heat out all night and can run 4 to 6 degrees lower, which puts the surface at or below freezing. Expect black ice at the creek crossing, worst at the bottom. Slow before the cut, not in it, and no brake on the bridge deck. I can't verify the surface from here. Is there frost forming on the mirrors, or has the spray off the tires gone quiet?
h_subsidence_paved_lot: Stop. Don't drive across it. A 6 ft hole with cracking around it and water underneath means the void is larger than the hole: the pavement is bridging a washed-out cavity, and 78,000 lb on an axle at the edge is what finishes the collapse. Back up straight and keep every axle at least 30 ft from the crack line, farther if the ground is soft. The lot exit is closed until someone probes it; that is a two-hour wait against a dropped tractor. I can't verify where the void ends from here. How far out does the cracking run, and is the pavement around it flat or already dished?
